q.intro.text: Three shops sell trail mix by weight. Their price lists are on the wall.

q.ask.text: At which shop is the cost proportional to the weight: the same price for every pound?

e.intro.text: Shop C. Six pounds for fifteen dollars, two pounds for five dollars, three pounds for seven fifty. Four steps. Press each one: the picture moves first, then the notation.

e.s0.text: Every row is one point: pounds across, dollars up. The row six pounds, fifteen dollars, is the point six, fifteen.

e.s1.text: Dollars divided by pounds, in the same order in every row. Fifteen divided by six, five divided by two, and seven fifty divided by three all give two point five. One rate, so the three points sit on one ray from zero, zero.

e.s2.text: k is two point five dollars per pound: the cost of one pound. On the graph it is the point one, two point five: one pound across, two dollars fifty up.

e.s3.text: Cost equals k times pounds: c equals two point five p. It fits every row, and zero pounds too: two point five times zero is zero, so the line starts at zero, zero.

e.why.text: Quick check: why divide in every row, not just the first two?

e.w-ok.text: Yes. Proportional means one multiplier for every row, so every row has to pass.

e.w-two.text: Not always. A table can agree in its first two rows and break in the third. Every row has to pass.

e.w-order.text: Keep one order in every row: dollars divided by pounds. Mixing the order compares different things.

t.intro.text: Gas from one pump: four gallons for fourteen dollars, ten gallons for thirty five, six gallons for twenty one. I plot the rows and divide the first two. Then it's your turn.

t.div.text: Divide the last row: dollars divided by gallons. How many dollars per gallon?

t.d-ok.text: Yes: twenty one divided by six is three point five. All three rows give three fifty per gallon, so they share one ray.

t.d-flip.text: That is gallons divided by dollars, the other order. Keep dollars divided by gallons, as in the other rows.

t.d-total.text: Twenty one is the total for six gallons. Divide it by six.

t.unit.text: Which point of the graph shows k, the price of one gallon?

t.u-ok.text: Yes: one, three point five. One gallon across, three fifty up. It sits between two grid lines, so the table is the easier place to read it.

t.u-swap.text: Order matters: gallons first, dollars second.

t.u-row.text: That is a whole row. k is the cost of one gallon.

t.u-other.text: Go to one gallon across. How many dollars up?

t.write.text: Now write the rule, with g for gallons and c for the cost. Which equation fits every row?

t.w-ok.text: Yes: c equals three point five g. Check a row: three point five times four is fourteen.

t.w-flip.text: Test it with a row: four gallons would give g equals three point five times fourteen, forty nine. The cost is the output: c equals three point five g.

t.w-add.text: Test it with a row: four plus three point five is seven point five, not fourteen. k multiplies: c equals three point five g.

t.zero.text: The pump starts at zero gallons, zero dollars. How do you check that row?

t.z-ok.text: Yes. Zero divided by zero has no value, so a zero row is checked by multiplying: three point five times zero is zero. It fits, and the ray starts at zero, zero.

t.z-zero.text: Zero divided by zero has no value: every number times zero is zero. Multiply instead: three point five times zero is zero.

t.z-reject.text: The row is fine. You can't divide there, so multiply: three point five times zero is zero. It fits.

t.cb-right.text: At the start you picked Shop C, and you were right: every row gives two fifty per pound. Now you can show why the others fail.

t.cb-a.text: At the start you picked Shop A. Its first two rows give three dollars per pound, but its last row gives two fifty. You prove it next.

t.cb-b.text: At the start you picked Shop B. Its prices go up by two dollars each time, but seven divided by two is three point five, and eleven divided by six is less than two: no single multiplier. Shop C was the proportional one.

t.cb-none.text: Back to the three shops: Shop C was the proportional one, two fifty for every pound.

p.intro.text: Riley says: Shop A is proportional. One pound costs three dollars and two pounds cost six: double the pounds, double the price. Is Riley right?

p.test.text: Let's test it. Build the argument and see where it leads.

p.prove.text: Now prove it. Fill each because with the reason that makes the line true.

p.c1.text: Rows one and two give three dollars per pound, because three divided by one is three, and six divided by two is three.

p.c2.text: But row three gives two fifty per pound, because ten divided by four is two point five.

p.c3.text: So no single multiplier fits every row, because one row that breaks the rule is enough. Shop A is not proportional.

p.x-double.text: That is Riley's check. Doubling once can only rule proportionality out, never prove it.

p.x-most.text: Most is not all. One row with another rate is enough to break it.

p.x-other.text: True, but it is the reason for a different line.

p.done.text: That's a proof: three claims, each with its reason, and the graph backs every one. Riley's doubling check passed, and Shop A still is not proportional.
